planting.note: Root short stem cuttings bearing a leaf whorl directly in barely damp, well-drained mix; the small succulent leaves rot quickly if cuttings are kept wet.

directions: This diminutive creeping species carries small, round to oval, fleshy leaves arranged in tight whorls of three or four along thread-like trailing stems, giving the plant its coin-leaf and four-leaf common names. Unlike the similarly whorl-leaved Peperomia quadrifolia, which is confined to the Americas, this species occurs pantropically across the Pacific, Africa, and the New World, making it a familiar sight in Hawaiian and Old World epiphyte collections as well. Grow in bright, indirect light with high humidity and let the mix dry slightly between waterings, since the tiny leaves store some moisture but have little buffer against rot. Its fine, mat-forming habit suits terrariums, shallow dish gardens, and mounted epiphyte displays better than a standard pot.
sources: specialty terrarium and epiphyte plant nurseries

planting.note: Let leaf or stem cuttings callus for a day before setting in gritty, fast-draining succulent mix, which prevents rot in the fleshy tissue while roots form.

directions: A Peruvian succulent-leaved species that clusters upright, gray-green stems set with thick, fleshy leaves bearing a pronounced angular ridge running along their length, a sharper and more faceted profile than the rounded pouch-shaped leaves of its relative Peperomia dolabriformis. Like other members of this Andean succulent group it stores water in its leaf tissue, so it thrives on bright light and infrequent, thorough watering with a long dry-down between soakings. It is more tolerant of direct sun than thin-leaved terrarium peperomias and should be grown in a mineral, cactus-style mix rather than standard peat-based potting soil. Its compact clustering habit and sculptural leaf shape make it a collector favorite alongside graveolens and ferreyrae.

planting.note: Root leaf or stem cuttings in moist, well-drained mix under warm, humid conditions; the fuzzy leaf surface benefits from good airflow to prevent fungal spotting.

directions: Native to Ecuadorian cloud forest, this species carries dark olive-green, heart-to-ovate leaves with a distinctly velvety, pubescent surface and pale silvery veining, set on reddish, upright-to-sprawling stems. The fuzzy leaf texture separates it at a glance from the smooth, deeply quilted foliage of the closely related Peperomia caperata group, and it also prefers steadier moisture and higher humidity than the more drought-tolerant succulent-leaved peperomias. Grow in bright, indirect light and keep the mix lightly and evenly moist rather than letting it dry hard, since cloud-forest origin makes it less forgiving of prolonged drought than desert-adapted species in the genus. Its compact rosette habit and unusual leaf texture make it a good centerpiece for a humid terrarium or enclosed cabinet.

planting.note: Root stem cuttings in water or moist mix; this species roots and trails vigorously from nearly any node.

directions: Native from Mexico through the Caribbean and into South America, this trailing to scrambling species bears smooth, glossy, oval leaves in opposite pairs along semi-succulent reddish stems, a plain-green counterpart to the more heavily marked trailing peperomias in cultivation. Its glabrous, unpatterned foliage tolerates lower light than variegated trailers, since there is no white or cream sectoring to fade or scorch, though the densest growth and glossiest leaf color still come with bright, indirect light. Let the mix dry moderately between waterings, as the fleshy stems and leaves store some moisture but decline quickly if left waterlogged. Its vigorous, easy-care trailing habit suits hanging baskets and shelf displays where a simpler, uniformly green cascade is wanted.

planting.note: Let leaf or stem cuttings callus briefly before inserting into gritty, fast-draining succulent mix to root.

directions: A Peruvian succulent species in the same collector-prized group as Peperomia graveolens and Peperomia ferreyrae, bearing thick, plump, oval to boat-shaped leaves in a cool blue-gray-green rather than the ruby red of graveolens, clustered on short upright stems. The dusty blue leaf tone and rounder, less sharply keeled profile distinguish it from both graveolens and the more angular dolabriformis and angulata. Give it full sun to bright light, since strong light keeps the compact clustering habit tight and intensifies the blue-gray coloring, and let the mineral, fast-draining mix dry out fully between thorough waterings. Its small size and striking color make it well suited to windowsill succulent collections alongside other semi-succulent peperomias.

planting.note: Root stem cuttings in gritty, fast-draining succulent mix; keep barely moist until new growth confirms rooting.

directions: Another Peruvian succulent species valued by collectors, this low, spreading peperomia bears thick, rounded leaves that deepen to a wine-red to bronze cast under strong light, fading toward green if grown too dark. Its trailing-to-mounding habit and smaller, more rounded leaf shape set it apart from the upright, banana-shaped leaves of dolabriformis and the ridged foliage of angulata within the same succulent-leaved group. Grow in full sun to very bright indirect light in a mineral, cactus-style mix, and let the soil dry completely between waterings, since the fleshy leaves hold enough reserve moisture to tolerate extended drought. Its low, spreading form and rich coloration make it a good choice for shallow succulent bowls and mixed collector displays.

planting.note: Root stem cuttings in moist, well-drained mix under warm, humid conditions typical of its Andean cloud-forest origin.

directions: Native to Andean cloud forest in Peru and Ecuador, this species takes its name from the three prominent longitudinal veins that run the length of its thin-textured, ovate leaves, set on slender reddish stems in a low, spreading rosette. Unlike the thick, water-storing foliage of dolabriformis or fosteri, its thinner leaves need steadier moisture and higher humidity, more in line with the care given to caperata or marmorata types. Grow in bright, indirect light and keep the mix lightly moist, allowing only the top layer to dry between waterings rather than a long full dry-down. Its compact, patterned foliage and manageable size make it a good fit for terrariums or small humid enclosures.
